cover.title: Operating Model Assessment Toolkit
cover.subtitle: CTO Consulting  |  Business Analysis Practice
cover.purpose: A structured toolkit for an exhaustive assessment of how an organisation delivers value: its strategy, customers, services, processes, capabilities, structure, governance, people, culture, performance management, technology, data, suppliers, locations, risk and compliance, finances and change capability. It combines a 157-question maturity diagnostic across 17 dimensions with the planning tools, current-state inventories, analysis and outputs needed to move from evidence to a prioritised set of recommendations.

steps.text: Complete the Engagement tab: client details, objectives, scope, hypotheses, design principles and assessment settings.
Register stakeholders, tailor the Interview Guides and issue the Document Requests list.
Run interviews and workshops, review documents and populate the current-state inventories (Capabilities, Processes, Org Structure, Decision Rights, Applications, Suppliers, Locations, Cost Baseline).
Score each question on the Assessment tab (current and target maturity, 1–5 or N/A) against the Maturity Model and 'What good looks like'. Record the evidence reviewed and your confidence in it.
Log findings and root causes on the Findings tab, validate them with stakeholders and review the Dashboard.
Describe the current and target state and key shifts on Current vs Target; log, score and sequence recommendations.
Add questions by inserting rows inside a dimension block and copying the formulas down. Dropdown values and span benchmarks are maintained on the Lists tab.

workbookMap.purpose: Client details, objectives, scope, hypotheses, design principles and assessment settings.
The 17 dimensions, definitions and mapping to recognised frameworks, plus the assessment approach.
Five-level maturity descriptors for each dimension.
Stakeholder register, influence and interest, and interview schedule.

69 pre-populated document and data requests with tracking.
157-question maturity diagnostic with evidence, confidence, gap and RAG.
Level 1 / Level 2 business capability map with importance, maturity and priority heat map.
Value streams and processes with documentation, automation and performance data.
Workforce mix, spans of control, layers and cost by business unit.
RAPID matrix for key decisions with checks for missing or multiple deciders.
Application portfolio with TIME classification and support expiry.
Supplier register with segmentation, expiry and dependency risk.
Site footprint, utilisation, leases and property cost.
Operating cost by business unit and cost type, cost per FTE and change spend.
Findings log with evidence, root cause, impact and severity.
Maturity profile, gaps, RAG, findings, recommendation profile and charts.
Current state, target state and key shifts for each dimension.
Recommendations scored by value and ease, categorised and sequenced by horizon.
Dropdown values, span-of-control benchmarks and importance weights.

cover.ragNote: RAG ratings compare target and current maturity using the thresholds on the Engagement tab (defaults: Red when the gap is 1.5 or more, Amber from 0.75, otherwise Green).

maturityScale.name: Initial
maturityScale.label: 1 – Initial
maturityScale.description: Ad hoc, undocumented and person-dependent. Outcomes are unpredictable and largely reactive.

maturityScale.name: Developing
maturityScale.label: 2 – Developing
maturityScale.description: Some practices are defined but applied inconsistently. Limited measurement; still largely reactive.

maturityScale.name: Defined
maturityScale.label: 3 – Defined
maturityScale.description: Practices are documented, standardised and applied consistently across the organisation.

maturityScale.name: Managed
maturityScale.label: 4 – Managed
maturityScale.description: Practices are measured and actively managed against targets. Decisions are data-driven.

maturityScale.name: Optimised
maturityScale.label: 5 – Optimised
maturityScale.description: Continuous improvement is embedded. Leading practice that adapts quickly to change.

maturityScale.name: Not applicable
maturityScale.label: N/A – Not applicable
maturityScale.description: Not relevant to this organisation or outside the agreed scope. Excluded from averages.

settingsHelp.label: Default target maturity (1–5)
settingsHelp.help: Pre-fills the Target Maturity column on the Assessment tab. Overwrite individual questions where the target differs.

settingsHelp.label: RAG: Red when maturity gap is at least
settingsHelp.help: Gap = target minus current. Applied to questions and dimension averages.

settingsHelp.label: RAG: Amber when maturity gap is at least
settingsHelp.help: Gaps below this threshold are Green.

settingsHelp.label: Prioritisation threshold (Value and Ease, 1–5)
settingsHelp.help: Recommendations with Value and Ease at or above this score are Quick wins; high Value / low Ease are Strategic initiatives.

settingsHelp.label: Maximum management layers (CEO = layer 1)
settingsHelp.help: Org Structure flags business units whose deepest reporting line exceeds this.

settingsHelp.label: Contract / lease / support expiry warning (days)
settingsHelp.help: Flags suppliers, leases and applications approaching expiry.

settingsHelp.label: Application TIME fit threshold (1–5)
settingsHelp.help: Business and technical fit at or above this are 'high' when classifying applications as Tolerate, Invest, Migrate or Eliminate.

principleExample.rationale: Variation adds cost, risk and complexity without adding customer value.
principleExample.implications: Common processes and systems across business units; local variation requires a documented case.

frameworkIntro: 17 dimensions synthesised from the Operating Model Canvas (POLISM), McKinsey 7S, the Galbraith Star Model and TOGAF / BIZBOK business architecture.

dimensions.name: Strategy & Direction
dimensions.definition: The organisation's purpose, strategic objectives and the explicit choices the operating model must enable.
dimensions.subComponents: Purpose and vision; strategic objectives; strategic choices; external environment; design principles; strategy-to-execution alignment; ESG
dimensions.keyQuestion: Is it clear what the operating model must deliver, and are the strategic choices explicit?
dimensions.standards: Balanced Scorecard; PESTLE / SWOT; Playing to Win; ASX Corporate Governance Principles

dimensions.name: Customers, Channels & Value Proposition
dimensions.definition: Who the organisation serves, what value it offers each segment, and how customers access and experience its services.
dimensions.subComponents: Segments; value proposition; customer journeys; channel strategy; omnichannel consistency; voice of customer; service standards; accessibility
dimensions.keyQuestion: Does the organisation understand and consistently deliver what its customers value, through the right channels?
dimensions.standards: Service design; NPS / CSAT / CES; WCAG 2.2; BIZBOK stakeholder mapping

dimensions.name: Products & Services
dimensions.definition: The portfolio of products and services the organisation delivers, and how that portfolio is owned, managed and evolved.
dimensions.subComponents: Service catalogue; portfolio performance; ownership; lifecycle; complexity; innovation pipeline; pricing and funding; product obligations
dimensions.keyQuestion: Is the portfolio of products and services clear, owned and actively managed for value?
dimensions.standards: Product lifecycle management; ITIL 4 service catalogue; ASIC design and distribution obligations (where applicable)

dimensions.name: Value Streams & Processes
dimensions.definition: The end-to-end value streams and business processes through which work flows to deliver outcomes.
dimensions.subComponents: Value streams; process architecture; ownership; documentation; standardisation; efficiency; automation; performance; hand-offs; embedded controls
dimensions.keyQuestion: Does work flow efficiently, consistently and under control from trigger to outcome?
dimensions.standards: APQC Process Classification Framework; BPMN 2.0; Lean; Six Sigma; process mining

dimensions.name: Business Capabilities
dimensions.definition: What the organisation must be able to do (independent of how), and the maturity of those abilities across people, process, technology and information.
dimensions.subComponents: Capability map; strategic importance; maturity; ownership; investment alignment; gaps; duplication; sourcing
dimensions.keyQuestion: Does the organisation have the capabilities its strategy needs, and is investment focused on the right ones?
dimensions.togaf: BIZBOK capability map; TOGAF capability-based planning

dimensions.name: Organisation Structure & Roles
dimensions.definition: How people and work are grouped, the reporting lines, spans and layers, and the clarity of roles and accountabilities.
dimensions.subComponents: Structural archetype; spans of control; layers; centralisation vs devolution; shared services and CoEs; role clarity; duplication; interfaces; agility
dimensions.keyQuestion: Is the structure aligned to strategy, lean, and clear about who is accountable for what?
dimensions.standards: Spans and layers analysis; organisation design archetypes

dimensions.name: Governance & Decision Rights
dimensions.definition: The bodies, delegations, policies and decision rights that direct and control the organisation.
dimensions.subComponents: Governance framework; committee effectiveness; delegations; decision rights; decision speed; policy framework; oversight; three lines; transparency
dimensions.keyQuestion: Are decisions made by the right people, at the right level, in a timely and accountable way?
dimensions.standards: ASX Corporate Governance Principles; PGPA Act 2013 (Commonwealth entities); COBIT 2019; IIA Three Lines Model; RAPID / RACI

dimensions.name: People, Workforce & Skills
dimensions.definition: The size, mix, skills, capacity and management of the workforce needed to deliver the operating model.
dimensions.subComponents: Workforce planning; workforce mix; capacity; skills; critical roles and succession; attraction and retention; performance; reward; WHS; engagement
dimensions.keyQuestion: Does the organisation have the right people, with the right skills, in the right numbers, at the right cost?
dimensions.standards: Strategic workforce planning; SFIA (digital skills); Work Health and Safety Act 2011 and psychosocial hazard regulations

dimensions.name: Culture, Leadership & Behaviours
dimensions.definition: The shared values, leadership style and everyday behaviours that determine how work actually gets done.
dimensions.subComponents: Values and behaviours; culture diagnosis; leadership; accountability; collaboration; customer centricity; psychological safety; risk culture; change readiness
dimensions.keyQuestion: Do culture and leadership enable, or undermine, the intended operating model?
dimensions.standards: Culture diagnostics; 360-degree feedback; risk culture assessments

dimensions.name: Performance Management & Planning
dimensions.definition: How the organisation plans, sets targets, measures performance and uses information to steer.
dimensions.subComponents: Planning cycle; KPI framework; cascade; management reporting; performance forums; target setting; incentive alignment; data for performance; external reporting
dimensions.keyQuestion: Does the organisation know how it is performing and act on that information?

dimensions.name: Technology & Applications
dimensions.definition: The applications, infrastructure, architecture and technology operating model that enable the business.
dimensions.subComponents: Technology strategy; enterprise architecture; application portfolio; technical debt; infrastructure and cloud; integration; IT operating model; ITSM; digital, automation and AI; tech investment; end-user tools
dimensions.keyQuestion: Is technology fit for purpose today, and an enabler rather than a constraint for the future?
dimensions.standards: TOGAF; ITIL 4; COBIT 2019; Gartner TIME model; FinOps; Technology Business Management (TBM)

dimensions.name: Data, Information & Analytics
dimensions.definition: How data and information are governed, managed, protected and used to generate insight.
dimensions.subComponents: Data strategy; data governance; data quality; master data; analytics; records management; privacy; classification; AI readiness
dimensions.keyQuestion: Is data trusted, protected and used as an asset for decision making?
dimensions.standards: DAMA-DMBOK; Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles; ISO 15489 records management; ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management)

dimensions.name: Suppliers, Partners & Sourcing
dimensions.definition: The external organisations the operating model relies on, and how they are selected, contracted, managed and governed.
dimensions.subComponents: Sourcing strategy; supplier register; contract management; performance; concentration and dependency risk; procurement process; partnerships; third-party risk
dimensions.keyQuestion: Are external dependencies deliberate, well managed and resilient?
dimensions.standards: Kraljic matrix; ISO 44001 collaborative relationships; APRA CPS 230 (material service providers); Commonwealth Procurement Rules

dimensions.name: Locations & Physical Assets
dimensions.definition: Where work is performed, the property and physical assets used, and the workplace model.
dimensions.subComponents: Location footprint; workplace model; utilisation; property costs and leases; site resilience; physical assets; physical security; environmental footprint
dimensions.keyQuestion: Is the physical footprint aligned to customers, talent, cost and resilience needs?
dimensions.standards: ISO 55001 asset management; NABERS; hybrid work frameworks

dimensions.name: Risk, Compliance, Security & Resilience
dimensions.definition: How the organisation identifies and manages risk, meets its obligations, protects information and remains resilient.
dimensions.subComponents: ERM framework; risk appetite; risk registers; obligations register; compliance management; controls; cyber security; business continuity; incidents; audit; fraud; ESG and climate risk
dimensions.keyQuestion: Is the organisation operating within its risk appetite and meeting its obligations, and can it withstand disruption?
dimensions.standards: ISO 31000; ISO 37301; ISO/IEC 27001; ISO 22301; ASD Essential Eight; APRA CPS 230 / CPS 234; PSPF; AASB S2

dimensions.name: Finance, Funding & Cost Model
dimensions.definition: The cost base, funding model, budgeting and financial controls that resource the operating model.
dimensions.subComponents: Cost baseline; cost-to-serve; cost structure; budgeting and forecasting; funding model; cost allocation; investment governance; financial controls; value for money
dimensions.keyQuestion: Is the cost of the operating model understood, affordable and directed at the highest-value activity?
dimensions.togaf: Not explicitly covered (cost of capabilities and portfolio)
dimensions.standards: Activity-based costing; Technology Business Management (TBM); zero-based budgeting

dimensions.name: Change, Transformation & Continuous Improvement
dimensions.definition: The organisation's ability to prioritise, deliver and embed change and to improve continuously.
dimensions.subComponents: Portfolio management; delivery methodology; delivery performance; change capacity; change management; benefits realisation; business analysis; continuous improvement; innovation; lessons learned
dimensions.keyQuestion: Can the organisation move from its current to its target operating model and sustain the change?
dimensions.standards: PRINCE2; MSP; P3O; Agile / SAFe; Prosci ADKAR; BABOK v3; Lean

approach.activities: Confirm objectives, scope, sponsor and success criteria. Identify stakeholders, issue the document request and schedule interviews. Agree design principles and assessment settings.
approach.outputs: Engagement charter; stakeholder map; document request

approach.activities: Review documents and data; run interviews, workshops and site visits; build the capability, process, organisation, decision rights, application, supplier, location and cost baselines.
approach.tabs: Interview Guides; Capabilities; Processes; Org Structure; Decision Rights; Applications; Suppliers; Locations; Cost Baseline
approach.outputs: Evidence base; current-state inventories and baselines

approach.activities: Score current and target maturity for every question with evidence and confidence ratings. Identify findings and root causes and validate them with stakeholders.
approach.outputs: Maturity profile; validated findings; heat maps

approach.activities: Describe the target state and key shifts for each dimension against the design principles. Develop and prioritise recommendations by value and ease.
approach.outputs: Target operating model directions; prioritised recommendations

approach.activities: Sequence recommendations into horizons, confirm dependencies, owners and indicative costs, and present to the sponsor and executive.

All: Ad hoc, undocumented and person-dependent. Outcomes are unpredictable and largely reactive.
Some practices are defined but applied inconsistently. Limited measurement; still largely reactive.
Practices are documented, standardised and applied consistently across the organisation.
Practices are measured and actively managed against targets. Decisions are data-driven.
Continuous improvement is embedded. Leading practice that adapts quickly to change.
D01: No articulated strategy, or it exists only in the heads of a few leaders. Priorities shift frequently.
Strategy documented but high level. Objectives are unclear or unprioritised; awareness is limited beyond the executive.
Clear strategy with measurable objectives and agreed design principles, cascaded into business plans.
Strategy drives portfolio, budget and operating model decisions. Progress reviewed quarterly and adjusted.
Adaptive, evidence-led strategy informed by continuous scanning. The whole organisation understands and contributes to it.
D02: Limited understanding of customers. Services are designed around internal structures.
Basic segmentation. Feedback is collected but rarely acted upon; channels are managed in silos.
Defined segments, value propositions and key journeys. Channel strategy and voice-of-customer program in place.
Journeys owned and measured end to end. Consistent omnichannel experience; insight drives service change.
Customer-centric by design. Predictive insight personalises services and customers co-design improvements.
D03: No complete view of products and services. Ownership is unclear.
Catalogue exists but is incomplete. Performance data is partial and launches are ad hoc.
Complete catalogue with owners, a defined lifecycle process and tracked performance.
Portfolio actively managed on value and cost, with regular rationalisation and a strategy-linked pipeline.
Portfolio continuously optimised using customer and financial insight; rapid test-and-learn development.
D04: Processes are undocumented and person-dependent, with high variation and rework.
Some processes documented. Ownership is functional and measurement is limited.
Process architecture defined. Key processes documented, owned and measured with KPIs.
End-to-end process owners manage performance. Processes are standardised and automation is applied systematically.
Processes continuously optimised using data (e.g. process mining), with intelligent automation at scale.
D05: No capability view. Investment is decided project by project.
A capability map has been drafted but is not used in decision making.
Endorsed capability map with named owners and a maturity assessment.
Capability-based planning drives investment, architecture and sourcing decisions.
The capability model is the common language for strategy, architecture, investment and performance.
D06: Structure has evolved organically. Roles are unclear and duplication is significant.
Structure documented with some role clarity. Spans and layers have not been analysed.
Structure aligned to strategy with a documented rationale. Roles defined; spans and layers within broad norms.
Structure optimised (spans, layers, shared services) and reviewed regularly, with strong cross-unit interfaces.
Adaptive structure that reconfigures around priorities with minimal disruption.
D07: Governance is informal. Decisions are escalated or made inconsistently; delegations are out of date.
Committees exist but overlap. Decision rights are unclear and delegations are poorly understood.
Governance framework and delegations defined. Committees have terms of reference; key decision rights are defined.
Governance is effective and efficient. Decisions are timely and made at the right level; the three lines operate well.
Governance is continuously reviewed. Decision making is agile, transparent and data-driven.
D08: Workforce management is reactive, with limited workforce data.
Basic workforce reporting. Skills gaps are known anecdotally and development is ad hoc.
Workforce plan and skills framework in place. Performance and development processes are consistent.
Strategic workforce planning is integrated with business planning. Talent is actively managed; engagement is high.
Predictive workforce analytics and agile deployment of talent. Recognised employer of choice.
D09: Values are not defined or not lived. Trust is low and behaviours are siloed.
Values are defined but inconsistently demonstrated. Culture is not measured.
Culture is measured and the desired shifts are defined. Leadership development is in place.
Leaders role-model desired behaviours. Culture is reinforced through hiring, reward and recognition.
Culture is a source of advantage, with high psychological safety and continuous learning.
D10: Few or no KPIs. Reporting is ad hoc and manual.
KPIs exist but are mainly financial or activity-based. Reporting is lagging and manual.
Balanced KPI framework cascaded through the organisation. Integrated planning cycle and regular performance forums.
Automated, trusted reporting. Performance information drives decisions and resource allocation.
Real-time, predictive performance insight. Continuous planning and adaptive targets.
D11: Fragmented, ageing technology with no strategy. IT is reactive.
Technology strategy exists. Application inventory is partial, technical debt is significant and architecture governance is limited.
Enterprise architecture practice and standards in place. Application portfolio managed; ITSM processes defined.
Technology aligned to capabilities. Technical debt actively reduced; mature cloud and integration platforms; strong business–IT partnership.
Technology is a strategic enabler. Product-based delivery, embedded automation and AI, and continuous modernisation.
D12: Data is siloed and of poor quality, with no ownership.
Some data governance. Quality issues are known; reporting relies on manual extraction.
Data governance framework with named owners and stewards. Quality measured for critical data elements.
Trusted single sources of truth and self-service analytics. Privacy and records are well managed.
Data is a strategic asset. Advanced analytics and AI drive decisions; the data culture is pervasive.
D13: No supplier register. Contracts are unmanaged and relationships transactional.
Supplier register exists. Basic contract management; limited performance measurement.
Sourcing strategy defined and suppliers segmented. Performance reviewed for key suppliers.
Strategic supplier relationships managed. Third-party risk, including exit plans, is actively managed and value tracked.
Ecosystem partnerships co-create value. Sourcing is continuously optimised.
D14: Footprint is historical and not aligned to strategy. Property costs are not visible.
Site and lease data captured. Limited utilisation analysis.
Footprint strategy and workplace model defined. Utilisation is measured.
Footprint optimised to customers, talent and cost. Site resilience is tested.
Flexible, data-driven footprint. Workplace continuously adapted; environmental footprint minimised.
D15: Risk and compliance managed reactively. Obligations not mapped; cyber security immature.
Risk framework documented but registers maintained inconsistently. Obligations partially mapped.
ERM framework operating. Obligations register and control library in place; cyber and BCM programs established.
Integrated risk, compliance and assurance. Controls tested, appetite drives decisions, resilience tested.
Risk intelligence informs strategy. Proactive regulatory engagement and continuous control monitoring.
D16: Costs visible only at general ledger level. Budgeting is incremental.
Cost-centre reporting and basic budgeting. Limited understanding of cost-to-serve.
Cost baseline by business unit and capability. Driver-based budgeting and consistent business cases.
Cost-to-serve informs decisions. Funding aligned to the operating model; benefits tracked.
Dynamic resource allocation, value-based funding and continuous efficiency.
D17: Change managed project by project with no portfolio view. Delivery track record is poor.
PMO established. Methods defined but inconsistently applied; benefits rarely tracked.
Portfolio prioritised against strategy. Standard delivery and change methods; benefits registers maintained.
Portfolio managed dynamically. Change capacity managed and benefits consistently realised.
Continuous transformation capability. Improvement and innovation embedded; the organisation learns and adapts rapidly.

questions.question: Is there a clearly articulated purpose, vision and mission that is understood across the organisation?
questions.good: Purpose and vision are documented and current. Staff at all levels can explain them and how their work contributes.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Strategic plan; vision and mission statements; staff engagement survey results

questions.question: Are strategic objectives specific, measurable and time-bound, with clear priorities and trade-offs?
questions.good: A small number of prioritised objectives with measures, targets and owners, plus explicit statements of what the organisation will not do.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Strategic or corporate plan; board papers

questions.question: Has the organisation made explicit choices about where it operates, whom it serves and how it creates value?
questions.good: Documented choices on target segments, services, channels and sources of advantage that directly inform operating model design.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Strategy documents; market analysis; business cases

questions.question: Does the strategy reflect a current understanding of the external environment (market, regulatory, technology, economic, social)?
questions.good: Regular environmental scanning (e.g. PESTLE) feeds strategy refresh. Emerging regulatory and technology changes are anticipated.
questions.evidenceToRequest: PESTLE / SWOT analyses; horizon-scanning reports; regulatory change updates

questions.question: Are there agreed operating model design principles that guide how the organisation is structured and operates?
questions.good: Six to ten principles (e.g. 'customer first', 'standardise unless differentiating', 'digital by default') endorsed by the executive and used to test design decisions.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Operating model documentation; design principles; executive decisions

questions.question: Is there a clear line of sight from strategy to portfolios, business plans, budgets and individual objectives?
questions.good: Strategy cascades into business unit plans, the investment portfolio, budgets and individual performance plans with traceable links.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Business unit plans; portfolio register; budget; performance agreements

questions.question: How effectively is the strategy communicated to, and understood by, staff, partners and other stakeholders?
questions.good: Structured communication plan. Staff can articulate strategic priorities; progress is discussed through regular two-way engagement.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Internal communication plans; intranet content; engagement survey

questions.question: Is progress against the strategy reviewed regularly and the strategy adjusted in response to performance and change?
questions.good: Quarterly strategy reviews by the executive and board, with documented adjustments and re-prioritisation.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Board and executive minutes; strategy performance reports

questions.question: Are sustainability, ESG and social-licence considerations embedded in the strategy?
questions.good: ESG objectives integrated into the strategy with measures. Climate-related risks and opportunities identified and disclosed where required.
questions.evidenceToRequest: ESG / sustainability strategy; climate risk assessment; annual report

questions.question: Are customer or stakeholder segments clearly defined, with an understanding of their needs and value?
questions.good: Evidence-based segmentation describing the needs, behaviours, value and cost to serve of each segment.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Segmentation studies; customer research; CRM analysis

questions.question: Is the value proposition for each segment clearly articulated and differentiated?
questions.good: Documented value propositions per segment, tested with customers and reflected in services and channels.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Value proposition documents; brand strategy; customer research

questions.question: Have the key end-to-end customer journeys been mapped, including pain points and moments that matter?
questions.good: Priority journeys mapped from the customer's perspective, with pain points quantified and owners assigned.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Journey maps; service blueprints; complaints analysis

questions.question: Is there a deliberate channel strategy (digital, phone, face-to-face, partner) aligned to customer needs and cost to serve?
questions.good: Channel roles defined by segment and interaction type; digital first where appropriate; consistent experience across channels.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Channel strategy; channel volume and cost data; digital analytics
questions.stakeholders: CX lead; Digital lead; Contact centre manager

questions.question: Do customers receive a consistent experience and consistent information across channels?
questions.good: Single view of the customer and a shared knowledge base across channels. Customers do not need to repeat themselves.
questions.evidenceToRequest: CRM architecture; knowledge management system; mystery shopping results

questions.question: Are customer feedback, complaints and satisfaction systematically captured, analysed and acted upon?
questions.good: Closed-loop voice-of-customer program (NPS / CSAT / CES) with root-cause analysis and evidence of changes made.
questions.evidenceToRequest: VoC reports; complaints register; NPS / CSAT trends

questions.question: Are customer service standards and commitments defined, published and measured?
questions.good: Published service charter or SLAs, with performance reported and remediation when targets are missed.

questions.question: Does the organisation use customer data and insight to design and improve services?
questions.good: Customer analytics informs product, service and channel decisions; insights are shared across teams.

questions.question: Are services accessible and inclusive for all customer groups, including customers experiencing vulnerability?
questions.good: Accessibility standards (e.g. WCAG 2.2 AA) met; vulnerable customer policy in place; inclusive design practised.

questions.question: Is there a complete, current catalogue of the products and services the organisation delivers (external and internal)?
questions.good: A single authoritative catalogue with owners, descriptions, customers, channels and service levels.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Product / service catalogue; internal service catalogue

questions.question: Is the performance, value or profitability of each product or service known?
questions.good: Revenue or value, cost, volumes and customer outcomes tracked for each product or service.

questions.question: Does every product or service have an accountable owner with end-to-end responsibility?
questions.good: Named owners accountable for outcomes, lifecycle and performance.

questions.question: Is there a defined lifecycle process for designing, launching, changing and retiring products and services?
questions.good: Stage-gated lifecycle with criteria for launch, review and retirement, applied consistently.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Product lifecycle process; product committee minutes

questions.question: Is portfolio complexity actively managed (e.g. overlapping, legacy or low-value products rationalised)?
questions.good: Periodic rationalisation reviews. The cost of complexity is understood; legacy products are migrated or retired.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Rationalisation reviews; product counts over time

questions.question: Is there a pipeline of new or improved products and services linked to strategy and customer insight?
questions.good: Managed pipeline with prioritisation criteria, a test-and-learn approach and clear funding.

questions.question: Are pricing, fees or funding arrangements for services understood, justified and reviewed?
questions.good: Pricing and funding models linked to cost-to-serve and value, and reviewed at least annually.

questions.question: Are product-related regulatory obligations (e.g. consumer law, design and distribution) identified and met?
questions.good: Obligations mapped to each product with controls and monitoring (e.g. target market determinations where applicable).

questions.question: Have the organisation's end-to-end value streams been identified (e.g. request-to-resolve, procure-to-pay, hire-to-retire)?
questions.good: Value streams defined from trigger to outcome, with stages, stakeholders and value items.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Value stream maps; business architecture artefacts

questions.question: Is there a structured process architecture (Level 0 to Level 3) covering core and supporting processes?
questions.good: Documented process hierarchy aligned to a reference model (e.g. APQC PCF) and actively maintained.

questions.question: Do end-to-end processes have accountable owners with authority across organisational boundaries?
questions.good: Named end-to-end process owners with a mandate, performance measures and improvement responsibility.

questions.question: Are key processes documented, current and accessible to the people who perform them?
questions.good: Processes documented in a common notation (e.g. BPMN 2.0) in a central repository with version control and review dates.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Process maps; standard operating procedures; work instructions

questions.question: Are processes standardised across business units and locations where there is no reason for variation?
questions.good: Common processes adopted by default. Variations are deliberate, justified and documented.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Process comparisons across units; audit findings

questions.question: Are processes efficient, with minimal rework, hand-offs, delays and manual workarounds?
questions.good: Process performance analysed (cycle time, rework, touchpoints) and waste systematically removed using Lean methods.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Process metrics; time-and-motion studies; workaround inventory

questions.question: What level of automation is applied, and are automation opportunities (including RPA and AI) identified and prioritised?
questions.good: Automation pipeline with business cases. High-volume, rules-based work is automated, with controls over bots and AI.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Automation register; RPA / AI use-case inventory

questions.question: Are process KPIs (volume, cycle time, cost, quality, compliance) defined and monitored?
questions.good: Process dashboards reviewed regularly by owners, with targets and corrective action.

questions.question: Are hand-offs between teams, functions and third parties clearly defined and managed?
questions.good: Clear hand-off points, internal service agreements (OLAs) between teams, and minimal queues between steps.

questions.question: Are key risk and compliance controls embedded in processes rather than applied after the fact?
questions.good: Controls designed into processes, mapped to risks and obligations, and tested.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Control library; risk and control matrix (RCM)

questions.question: Does the organisation have a current business capability map describing what it does, independent of how?
questions.good: Levelled capability map (L1 to L3) endorsed by executives and used in planning and investment decisions.

questions.question: Have capabilities been classified by strategic importance and differentiation (differentiating vs commodity)?
questions.good: Each capability rated for strategic importance and differentiation, informing sourcing and investment.

questions.question: Has capability maturity been assessed across people, process, technology and information?
questions.good: Periodic, evidence-based maturity assessment with a target maturity for each capability.

questions.question: Is there a named owner for each capability, accountable for its performance and uplift?
questions.good: Capability owners identified with clear accountability and uplift plans.

questions.question: Is investment directed to the capabilities that matter most to the strategy?
questions.good: Portfolio investment mapped to capabilities, with spend weighted towards strategic gaps.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Investment portfolio mapped to capabilities; budget

questions.question: Are gaps between current and required capabilities identified, with plans to close them?
questions.good: Gap analysis linked to roadmap initiatives with timeframes and funding.

questions.question: Are capabilities duplicated across business units, and is any duplication deliberate?
questions.good: Duplication identified; consolidation or shared services considered where appropriate.

questions.question: Is there a deliberate decision on which capabilities are delivered in-house, shared, outsourced or partnered?
questions.good: Sourcing decisions follow a documented framework linked to differentiation, cost and risk.

questions.question: Is the organisational structure (functional, divisional, matrix, product / platform, network) aligned to the strategy and design principles?
questions.good: Structure explicitly linked to strategy with a documented rationale. Trade-offs are understood and managed.

questions.question: Are spans of control appropriate for the nature of the work?
questions.good: Spans within agreed benchmarks (see Lists tab); outliers are justified.
questions.evidenceToRequest: HR system extract (reporting lines); organisation charts

questions.question: Is the number of management layers appropriate for the organisation's size and complexity?
questions.good: Minimal layers between the CEO and the frontline (commonly 5 to 7 for large organisations); decisions are not slowed by hierarchy.

questions.question: Is there a clear, deliberate balance between centralised, shared and devolved functions?
questions.good: The rationale for what is centralised versus local is documented; there are minimal shadow functions.

questions.question: Are shared services and centres of excellence used where they add value, with clear service agreements?
questions.good: Shared services operate with service catalogues, SLAs and customer satisfaction measures.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Shared services catalogue; SLAs; satisfaction surveys
questions.stakeholders: Shared services leads; Business unit heads

questions.question: Are roles, accountabilities and responsibilities clearly defined and understood?
questions.good: Current role descriptions and documented accountabilities, with little overlap or gaps between roles.

questions.question: Is there duplication of roles or activities across units (e.g. shadow finance, HR or IT teams)?
questions.good: Duplicated activity identified and deliberately resolved.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Activity analysis; organisation charts; cost centre data

questions.question: Are interfaces between organisational units clearly defined, with effective mechanisms for cross-unit work?
questions.good: Cross-functional teams, forums and operating agreements support end-to-end delivery.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Operating agreements; forum terms of reference

questions.question: Can the structure adapt quickly to changing priorities (e.g. through cross-functional or agile teams)?
questions.good: Mechanisms exist to form and re-form teams around priorities without full restructures.

questions.question: Is there a documented governance framework showing the governing bodies and committees and how they relate?
questions.good: Governance map with a clear hierarchy, purpose, membership and reporting lines for each body.

questions.question: Do governance forums have clear terms of reference, the right membership and effective agendas?
questions.good: Current terms of reference. Forums focus on decisions rather than information; effectiveness is reviewed periodically.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Terms of reference; agendas; minutes; effectiveness reviews

questions.question: Are financial and non-financial delegations documented, current and understood?
questions.good: Delegations instrument aligned to structure and risk appetite, reviewed annually and system-enforced where possible.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Delegations of authority schedule; system workflow rules

questions.question: Is it clear who recommends, agrees, decides and provides input on key decisions?
questions.good: Decision rights (e.g. RAPID or RACI) defined for key decisions, which are made at the lowest appropriate level.

questions.question: Are decisions made in a timely way, without excessive escalation or duplication of forums?
questions.good: Reasonable decision cycle times, little re-litigation of decisions and clear escalation thresholds.

questions.question: Is there a structured policy framework with ownership, review cycles and alignment to obligations?
questions.good: Policy hierarchy (policy, standard, procedure) with owners, review dates and attestation.

questions.question: Does the board and executive receive timely, decision-useful information on performance, risk and change?
questions.good: Integrated reporting to the board covering strategy, performance, risk and major programs.

questions.question: Are roles across the three lines (management, risk and compliance oversight, independent assurance) clear and effective?
questions.good: Clear separation of accountabilities between the first, second and third lines, with a coordinated assurance map.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Assurance map; risk framework; internal audit charter

questions.question: Are decisions, rationale and accountabilities recorded and traceable?
questions.good: Decision registers, minutes and action logs maintained and followed up.

questions.question: Is there a strategic workforce plan linking future capability needs to the strategy?
questions.good: Three-to-five-year workforce plan with supply and demand analysis, critical roles and actions.

questions.question: Is the workforce mix (permanent, fixed-term, contractor, outsourced, offshore) deliberate and cost-effective?
questions.good: Target workforce mix defined by capability; contractor reliance monitored and justified.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Headcount / FTE by employment type; contractor spend

questions.question: Is workforce capacity matched to demand, with visibility of utilisation and backlogs?
questions.good: Demand forecasting and capacity planning used; resources rebalanced as demand changes.

questions.question: Are current skills known, and are gaps against future needs identified?
questions.good: Skills framework and inventory in place; gaps quantified and addressed through development plans.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Skills framework; capability assessments; training records

questions.question: Are critical roles and key-person dependencies identified, with succession plans?
questions.good: Critical roles identified, with ready-now successors and captured knowledge.

questions.question: Can the organisation attract and retain the talent it needs?
questions.good: Competitive employee value proposition; turnover, time-to-fill and regretted losses within targets.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Turnover data; recruitment metrics; exit interview themes

questions.question: Is there an effective performance and development framework linked to objectives and behaviours?
questions.good: Regular performance conversations; objectives cascaded from strategy; development plans in place.

questions.question: Do reward and recognition mechanisms reinforce the desired outcomes and behaviours?
questions.good: Remuneration and incentives aligned to strategy, risk and behaviours; pay equity monitored.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Remuneration framework; incentive plans; pay equity analysis

questions.question: Are work health and safety risks, including psychosocial hazards, managed effectively?
questions.good: WHS management system in place; psychosocial risks identified and controlled in line with WHS regulations.
questions.evidenceToRequest: WHS reports; psychosocial risk assessments; incident data

questions.question: Is employee engagement measured and acted upon?
questions.good: Regular engagement surveys with action plans and visible follow-through.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Engagement survey results and action plans

questions.question: Are organisational values defined and translated into observable behaviours?
questions.good: Values embedded in recruitment, performance and recognition; behaviours are observable in practice.

questions.question: Has the current culture been diagnosed and compared with the culture needed to deliver the strategy?
questions.good: Culture diagnostic completed; priority culture shifts defined and tracked.

questions.question: Do leaders have the capability to lead through change and deliver the strategy?
questions.good: Leadership framework, development programs and 360-degree feedback; leaders role-model desired behaviours.

questions.question: Do people take ownership of outcomes, and are they held to account constructively?
questions.good: Clear expectations, consequences and recognition; issues raised and resolved without blame.

questions.question: Is there effective collaboration across teams and functions, or are silos evident?
questions.good: Cross-functional collaboration is the norm, with shared goals across units and little siloed behaviour.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Engagement survey; organisational network analysis; interviews

questions.question: Do staff make decisions with the customer or beneficiary outcome in mind?
questions.good: Customer outcomes feature in everyday decision making and in measures.

questions.question: Do staff feel safe to raise concerns, challenge ideas and report issues?
questions.good: High psychological safety scores; effective speak-up and whistleblower mechanisms.

questions.question: Is there a healthy risk culture in which risks are identified, escalated and managed openly?
questions.good: Risk culture assessed; risks and incidents reported promptly; lessons learned applied.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Risk culture survey; incident reporting trends

questions.question: How ready and able is the organisation to adopt change?
questions.good: Change fatigue understood, change capacity managed and a history of successful adoption.

questions.question: Is there an integrated planning cycle linking strategic, business, workforce and financial planning?
questions.good: Annual integrated planning calendar with clear inputs, outputs and decision points.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Planning calendar; business plans; budget process

questions.question: Is there a balanced set of KPIs (financial, customer, process, people, risk) aligned to the strategy?
questions.good: Balanced scorecard or equivalent with defined measures, targets, owners and data sources.

questions.question: Do KPIs and objectives cascade from enterprise to business unit, team and individual levels?
questions.good: Clear line of sight from enterprise goals to team and individual objectives (e.g. OKRs).

questions.question: Is management reporting timely, accurate, insightful and trusted?
questions.good: Automated, single-source reporting focused on insight and exceptions, with little manual effort.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Management reports; report inventory; production effort

questions.question: Are there regular forums where performance is reviewed and actions agreed?
questions.good: A rhythm of performance reviews at each level, with actions tracked to closure.

questions.question: Are targets stretching yet achievable, and based on evidence and benchmarks?
questions.good: Targets informed by baselines, benchmarks and capacity, and reviewed as conditions change.

questions.question: Are performance measures aligned with incentives and consequences?
questions.good: Incentives reward balanced performance, including risk and behaviours, not just financial outcomes.

questions.question: Is performance data reliable, with clear definitions and data ownership?
questions.good: KPI definitions documented, data lineage understood and data quality monitored.

questions.question: Are external and regulatory performance reporting obligations met efficiently?
questions.good: External reporting automated where possible, reconciled to internal reporting and delivered on time.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Annual report; regulatory returns; reporting calendar

questions.question: Is there a technology strategy aligned to the business strategy and target operating model?
questions.good: Current technology strategy with roadmap, principles and funding, endorsed by the executive.

questions.question: Is there an enterprise architecture function with current and target state architectures and standards?
questions.good: EA practice (e.g. TOGAF-based) with architecture governance, standards and reference architectures.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Architecture repository; standards; architecture review board minutes

questions.question: Is the application portfolio documented with ownership, cost, business fit and technical health?
questions.good: Complete application inventory with a TIME assessment (Tolerate, Invest, Migrate, Eliminate) and rationalisation plan.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Application inventory; CMDB extract; licence data

questions.question: Is technical debt (legacy, unsupported or end-of-life systems) known and managed?
questions.good: Technical debt quantified and prioritised; remediation funded in the roadmap.
questions.evidenceToRequest: End-of-life / end-of-support register; technical debt register

questions.question: Is the hosting model (on-premises, cloud, hybrid) fit for purpose, secure and cost-effective?
questions.good: Deliberate hosting strategy; cloud costs managed through FinOps; resilience tested.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Infrastructure architecture; cloud strategy; cloud cost reports

questions.question: Are systems integrated effectively, minimising manual re-keying and point-to-point interfaces?
questions.good: Integration platform or API strategy with reusable services and little manual re-keying.

questions.question: Is the IT operating model (plan-build-run, product teams, sourcing) clear and effective?
questions.good: Defined IT operating model with clear roles, sourcing and a business engagement model.
questions.evidenceToRequest: IT organisation chart; IT operating model; IT service catalogue

questions.question: Are IT services managed to agreed levels using recognised practices (e.g. ITIL 4)?
questions.good: Service catalogue, SLAs, incident, problem and change management, and service performance reporting.
questions.evidenceToRequest: ITSM reports; SLAs; major incident reviews

questions.question: Is the organisation using digital, automation and AI capabilities to improve services and efficiency, with appropriate governance?
questions.good: AI and automation strategy with a use-case pipeline, responsible AI governance and measured benefits.
questions.evidenceToRequest: AI strategy; AI use-case register; AI policy

questions.question: Is technology spend visible, benchmarked and aligned to business value?
questions.good: IT spend understood by run / grow / transform and by capability; business cases track benefits.
questions.evidenceToRequest: IT budget; IT cost model; benchmarks

questions.question: Do staff have the tools and devices they need to work effectively, including in hybrid settings?
questions.good: Modern collaboration tools, high user satisfaction and secure access from any location.
questions.evidenceToRequest: User satisfaction survey; device and tool inventory

questions.question: Is there a data strategy that treats data as an asset and supports business priorities?
questions.good: Endorsed data strategy with roadmap, funding and executive sponsorship.
questions.stakeholders: Chief Data Officer / data lead; CIO

questions.question: Is there a data governance framework with defined owners, stewards and decision forums?
questions.good: Data owners and stewards named for key domains; a data governance council operating.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Data governance framework; data owner register

questions.question: Is data quality measured and managed for critical data elements?
questions.good: Critical data elements identified; quality dimensions measured; issues remediated at source.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Data quality reports; data issue logs

questions.question: Is master data (customer, product, supplier, employee) managed as a single source of truth?
questions.good: Master data management approach in place, with minimal duplication and defined authoritative sources.

questions.question: Does the organisation have the analytics capability to generate insight for decisions?
questions.good: Self-service BI, advanced analytics capability and a data-driven decision culture.
questions.evidenceToRequest: BI platform inventory; analytics use cases

questions.question: Are information and records managed in line with legislative and business requirements?
questions.good: Records management policy, classification and retention and disposal schedules applied.

questions.question: Is personal information handled in line with privacy obligations (e.g. Privacy Act 1988 and the APPs)?
questions.good: Privacy management plan, privacy impact assessments and a tested data breach response plan.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Privacy policy; PIAs; data breach response plan

questions.question: Is data classified and protected according to its sensitivity?
questions.good: Classification scheme applied, controls proportionate to classification, access reviewed regularly.

questions.question: Is data of sufficient quality, accessibility and governance to support AI and advanced analytics?
questions.good: Data platforms, lineage and governance ready for AI use cases, with responsible AI controls in place.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Data platform architecture; AI readiness assessment

questions.question: Is there a sourcing strategy defining what is performed in-house, outsourced or delivered through partners?
questions.good: Sourcing decisions based on differentiation, capability, cost and risk, and reviewed periodically.

questions.question: Is there a complete register of suppliers with spend, services, criticality and contract details?
questions.good: Single supplier register with segmentation (e.g. strategic, leverage, bottleneck, non-critical).

questions.question: Are contracts actively managed, with clear obligations, performance measures and renewal dates?
questions.good: Contract management system; obligations tracked; renewals planned well in advance.

questions.question: Is supplier performance measured and managed through regular reviews?
questions.good: Supplier scorecards and performance reviews for strategic and critical suppliers.

questions.question: Are dependencies on critical or single-source suppliers (including fourth parties) understood and mitigated?
questions.good: Material service providers identified; exit and contingency plans in place and tested.

questions.question: Is the procurement process efficient, compliant and value-driven?
questions.good: Procurement policy aligned to applicable rules (e.g. Commonwealth Procurement Rules); reasonable cycle times.

questions.question: Are partnerships and ecosystem relationships used effectively to deliver the value proposition?
questions.good: Strategic partnerships with shared objectives, governance and measured value.

questions.question: Are third-party security, privacy and compliance risks assessed before and during engagement?
questions.good: Due diligence and ongoing monitoring of third-party controls (e.g. ISO/IEC 27001 certification, SOC 2 reports).

questions.question: Is the location footprint (offices, sites, service centres) aligned to customers, talent and cost?
questions.good: Footprint strategy based on customer proximity, talent pools and cost, with a documented rationale.

questions.question: Is there a deliberate workplace model (e.g. hybrid, activity-based working) supported by policy and technology?
questions.good: Workplace model defined, utilisation measured, and policy and tools support it.

questions.question: Is space utilisation measured and optimised?
questions.good: Utilisation tracked; surplus space consolidated or sub-let.

questions.question: Are property costs and lease commitments understood and managed in line with strategy?
questions.good: Lease expiries aligned to the footprint strategy; property cost per FTE benchmarked.

questions.question: Are critical sites resilient, with business continuity arrangements for site loss?
questions.good: Alternate sites or work-from-anywhere arrangements tested; critical infrastructure protected.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Business continuity plans; site risk assessments

questions.question: Are physical assets (equipment, fleet, infrastructure) managed across their lifecycle?
questions.good: Asset register and lifecycle management consistent with ISO 55001 principles.

questions.question: Are physical security controls appropriate to the sensitivity of people, information and assets on each site?
questions.good: Physical security risk assessed per site; access control and monitoring proportionate to risk.

questions.question: Is the environmental impact of locations and assets measured and managed?
questions.good: Scope 1 and 2 emissions measured; energy efficiency targets in place.

questions.question: Is there an enterprise risk management framework aligned to a recognised standard (e.g. ISO 31000)?
questions.good: ERM framework in operation, with risk appetite, taxonomy, assessment methodology and reporting.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Risk management framework; risk appetite statement

questions.question: Is risk appetite defined, measurable and used in decision making?
questions.good: Board-approved appetite with metrics and tolerances that are monitored, with breaches escalated.

questions.question: Are strategic, operational and project risks identified, assessed and actively managed?
questions.good: Current risk registers with owners, controls, treatment plans and regular review.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Enterprise and business unit risk registers

questions.question: Is there a complete register of legal, regulatory and contractual obligations mapped to owners and controls?
questions.good: Obligations register maintained, with regulatory change monitoring (e.g. aligned to ISO 37301).

questions.question: Is compliance monitored, tested and reported, with breaches managed and remediated?
questions.good: Compliance monitoring plan, breach register and timely regulator notification where required.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Compliance plan; breach register; regulator correspondence

questions.question: Are key controls documented, owned and tested for design and operating effectiveness?
questions.good: Control library mapped to risks; testing results reported; issues tracked to closure.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Control library; control testing results; RCSA

questions.question: Is cyber security maturity appropriate for the threat environment (e.g. Essential Eight, ISO/IEC 27001, NIST CSF)?
questions.good: Target maturity defined and achieved (e.g. Essential Eight Maturity Level 2 or higher); ISMS operating; incidents managed.
questions.evidenceToRequest: ISMS documentation; Essential Eight assessment; penetration test reports

questions.question: Can the organisation continue critical operations through disruption (e.g. ISO 22301; APRA CPS 230 where applicable)?
questions.good: Critical operations and tolerance levels defined; BCPs and disaster recovery tested; scenario exercises run.
questions.evidenceToRequest: BCPs; business impact analysis; DR test results; CPS 230 artefacts

questions.question: Are operational incidents and near misses captured, investigated and learned from?
questions.good: Incident management process with root-cause analysis and trend reporting.

questions.question: Is independent assurance risk-based, and are audit findings remediated on time?
questions.good: Risk-based internal audit plan; overdue actions tracked and reported to the Audit Committee.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Internal audit plan; audit reports; action tracker
questions.stakeholders: Head of Internal Audit; Audit Committee

questions.question: Are fraud, corruption and integrity risks managed?
questions.good: Fraud control plan, integrity framework and a whistleblower program in place and tested.

questions.question: Are climate-related and other ESG risks identified, managed and disclosed as required (e.g. AASB S2)?
questions.good: Climate risks integrated into ERM; disclosure obligations mapped and met.

questions.question: Is the cost base understood by business unit, capability, process and cost type?
questions.good: Cost baseline available at multiple cuts and reconciled to the financial statements.
questions.evidenceToRequest: General ledger extract; cost centre reports

questions.question: Is the cost to serve customers, products and channels known?
questions.good: Activity- or driver-based costing informs pricing, channel and service decisions.

questions.question: Is the cost structure (fixed vs variable; people vs non-people) appropriate and benchmarked?
questions.good: Cost structure benchmarked against peers, with flexibility to scale costs with demand.

questions.question: Is budgeting and forecasting timely, accurate and linked to strategy and performance?
questions.good: Driver-based budgets, rolling forecasts and variance analysis with commentary.

questions.question: Is the funding model (e.g. project vs product funding, appropriation, fee-for-service) aligned to how value is delivered?
questions.good: Funding model supports the operating model (e.g. persistent funding for product teams).

questions.question: Are shared costs allocated or charged back in a transparent and fair way?
questions.good: Transparent allocation methodology, understood by business units and driving the desired behaviour.

questions.question: Are investments assessed using consistent business cases and benefits tracking?
questions.good: Standard business case template, investment committee and post-investment reviews.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Business case template; investment committee papers

questions.question: Are financial controls, delegations and reporting robust?
questions.good: Strong control environment, clean audit opinions and a timely month-end close.
questions.evidenceToRequest: External audit reports; management letters; month-end timetable

questions.question: Does the organisation regularly assess efficiency and value for money?
questions.good: Efficiency reviews, benchmarking and savings targets tracked; productivity trends monitored.

questions.question: Is there a portfolio management function that prioritises, funds and oversees change initiatives?
questions.good: Single portfolio view with prioritisation criteria linked to strategy and regular portfolio reviews.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Portfolio register; prioritisation framework; portfolio reports

questions.question: Are delivery methods (agile, waterfall, hybrid) appropriate and consistently applied?
questions.good: Tailored delivery frameworks (e.g. PRINCE2, Agile / SAFe) with clear governance and stage gates.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Delivery framework; project governance; project status reports

questions.question: Are initiatives delivered on time and on budget, and do they achieve the expected outcomes?
questions.good: A high proportion of initiatives delivered within tolerance, with early escalation of issues.

questions.question: Is the volume of change managed against the organisation's capacity to absorb it?
questions.good: Change heat maps across business units; sequencing considers change saturation.

questions.question: Is structured change management applied to drive adoption (e.g. Prosci ADKAR)?
questions.good: Change impact assessments, stakeholder engagement, training and adoption metrics used on all major initiatives.
questions.evidenceToRequest: Change management framework; change impact assessments

questions.question: Are benefits defined, owned, tracked and realised after implementation?
questions.good: Benefits register with owners and baselines; benefits tracked beyond project close.

questions.question: Is business analysis capability mature enough to define needs and solutions effectively (e.g. BABOK v3)?
questions.good: Consistent BA practice with standards, templates, traceability and skilled practitioners.
questions.evidenceToRequest: BA framework; requirements artefacts; traceability matrices

questions.question: Is there an embedded continuous improvement culture and method (e.g. Lean, Six Sigma)?
questions.good: CI methods used by frontline teams; improvement ideas captured, prioritised and implemented.

questions.question: Does the organisation have mechanisms to identify, test and scale innovations?
questions.good: Innovation process with funding, experimentation and scaling pathways.

questions.question: Are lessons learned captured and applied to future initiatives?
questions.good: Lessons-learned repository used in planning; recurring issues decrease over time.

stakeholderExample.name: Jane Citizen
stakeholderExample.notes: Sees cross-unit hand-offs as the main constraint on service times.

interviewGuides.question: What are the organisation's most important priorities over the next three to five years, and how confident are you that it can deliver them?
interviewGuides.probe: Which priorities are most at risk, and why?

interviewGuides.question: How well does the information the board receives support decisions on strategy, performance and risk?
interviewGuides.probe: What would you like to see more or less of?

interviewGuides.question: How clear are the respective roles of the board, its committees and management?
interviewGuides.probe: Any areas where the board is drawn into operational matters?

interviewGuides.question: How would you describe the organisation's risk appetite and risk culture?
interviewGuides.probe: Recent examples where appetite shaped a decision.

interviewGuides.question: Where do you see the greatest operational, cyber or regulatory exposures?
interviewGuides.probe: How confident are you in the organisation's resilience?

interviewGuides.question: How effectively does the organisation deliver major change and realise the promised benefits?
interviewGuides.probe: Recent programs that succeeded or struggled.

interviewGuides.question: What would a successful operating model look like to the board in three years?
interviewGuides.probe: How would you know it had been achieved?

interviewGuides.question: What is the organisation trying to achieve, and what must the operating model do differently to get there?
interviewGuides.probe: What are the non-negotiables?

interviewGuides.question: What are the biggest barriers to executing the strategy today?
interviewGuides.probe: Are they structural, process, people, technology or cultural?

interviewGuides.question: Which capabilities are most critical to success, and where are the largest gaps?
interviewGuides.probe: Which capabilities should be built, bought or partnered?

interviewGuides.question: How are decisions made at the executive level, and where do decisions get stuck?
interviewGuides.probe: Examples of decisions that took too long or were revisited.

interviewGuides.question: How well do business units and functions work together to deliver end to end for customers?
interviewGuides.probe: Where do hand-offs break down?

interviewGuides.question: How is performance measured and managed across the organisation?
interviewGuides.probe: Which measures actually drive behaviour?

interviewGuides.question: What is the organisation's capacity and appetite for change over the next 12 to 24 months?
interviewGuides.probe: What else is competing for attention?

interviewGuides.question: What works well today and must be protected in any future operating model?
interviewGuides.probe: What would staff say is worth keeping?

interviewGuides.question: Describe your unit's purpose, key services and customers.
interviewGuides.probe: How has demand changed over the last two years?

interviewGuides.question: Walk me through the end-to-end process for your most important service. Where are the delays, hand-offs and rework?
interviewGuides.probe: What proportion of work needs rework or escalation?

interviewGuides.question: How clear are accountabilities between your unit and the other units you depend on?
interviewGuides.probe: Examples of work falling between the cracks.

interviewGuides.question: Which decisions can you make without escalation, and which should you be able to make?
interviewGuides.probe: How long do escalated decisions typically take?

interviewGuides.question: Do you have the right people, skills and capacity to meet demand?
interviewGuides.probe: Where are you relying on contractors or key individuals?

interviewGuides.question: How well do systems and data support your team's work, and what workarounds exist?
interviewGuides.probe: Spreadsheets, re-keying or shadow systems in use.

interviewGuides.question: Which KPIs do you manage to, and how are they used?
interviewGuides.probe: Do the measures reflect what matters to customers?

interviewGuides.question: What are the three changes that would most improve your unit's performance?
interviewGuides.probe: What has prevented them so far?

interviewGuides.question: What does a typical day look like, and what gets in the way of doing your job well?
interviewGuides.probe: How much time is lost to these issues each week?

interviewGuides.question: Where do you spend time on manual workarounds, rework or chasing information?
interviewGuides.probe: Can you show me an example?

interviewGuides.question: How clear is it who is responsible for what, and whom to escalate to?
interviewGuides.probe: What happens when something is unclear?

interviewGuides.question: How well do you understand the organisation's strategy and how your work contributes to it?
interviewGuides.probe: How is progress communicated to you?

interviewGuides.question: Which customer pain points do you see most often?
interviewGuides.probe: What would fix them?

interviewGuides.question: Do you have the training, tools and support you need?
interviewGuides.probe: What is missing?

interviewGuides.question: How comfortable do you feel raising concerns or suggesting improvements?
interviewGuides.probe: What happened the last time you did?

interviewGuides.question: If you could change one thing about how the organisation works, what would it be?
interviewGuides.probe: Why that change?

interviewGuides.question: How is the cost base structured, and how well is it understood by business unit and capability?
interviewGuides.probe: Can costs be traced to services and customers?

interviewGuides.question: Is the cost to serve customers, products and channels understood?
interviewGuides.probe: Which segments or channels are unprofitable or high cost?

interviewGuides.question: How are budgets set and resources allocated to strategic priorities?
interviewGuides.probe: How much of the budget is discretionary?

interviewGuides.question: How is investment governed, and are benefits tracked after delivery?
interviewGuides.probe: Examples of benefits that were or were not realised.

interviewGuides.question: How effective are delegations and financial controls?
interviewGuides.probe: Recent audit findings or control breaches.

interviewGuides.question: Where are the largest efficiency or cost-reduction opportunities?
interviewGuides.probe: What has been tried before?

interviewGuides.question: How reliable and timely is management and financial reporting?
interviewGuides.probe: How much manual effort goes into producing it?

interviewGuides.question: How well does the current structure support the strategy, and what are the main pain points?
interviewGuides.probe: When was the structure last reviewed?

interviewGuides.question: What does the workforce profile look like (headcount, mix, spans, layers, turnover)?
interviewGuides.probe: Can we obtain an HR system extract?

interviewGuides.question: Where are the critical skills gaps and key-person dependencies?
interviewGuides.probe: Which roles are hardest to fill?

interviewGuides.question: How would you describe the current culture, and what needs to shift?
interviewGuides.probe: What evidence supports that view?

interviewGuides.question: How do performance management and reward reinforce the desired outcomes and behaviours?
interviewGuides.probe: Any unintended consequences?

interviewGuides.question: How are WHS risks, including psychosocial hazards, managed?
interviewGuides.probe: Trends in incidents, claims or absenteeism.

interviewGuides.question: What is the organisation's track record with restructures and people change?
interviewGuides.probe: Lessons learned from previous changes.

interviewGuides.question: How well is the technology strategy aligned with the business strategy?
interviewGuides.probe: How are technology priorities set?

interviewGuides.question: What is the state of the application portfolio and technical debt?
interviewGuides.probe: Which systems are end-of-life or unsupported?

interviewGuides.question: How effectively are systems integrated, and where is data re-keyed?
interviewGuides.probe: Which interfaces fail most often?

interviewGuides.question: How is the IT function organised, and how does it engage with the business?
interviewGuides.probe: Plan-build-run, product teams or a mix?

interviewGuides.question: How mature are data governance, data quality and analytics?
interviewGuides.probe: Is there a trusted single source of truth for key data?

interviewGuides.question: What is the cyber security posture and target maturity?
interviewGuides.probe: Latest Essential Eight or ISO/IEC 27001 assessment results.

interviewGuides.question: How is the organisation approaching automation and AI, and how is it governed?
interviewGuides.probe: Use cases in production and their measured benefits.

interviewGuides.question: What are the largest technology risks to operations and to change delivery?
interviewGuides.probe: Single points of failure and key-person risks.

interviewGuides.question: How mature is the enterprise risk management framework, and how is it used in decision making?
interviewGuides.probe: Examples where risk information changed a decision.

interviewGuides.question: How are legal and regulatory obligations identified, owned and monitored?
interviewGuides.probe: Is there an obligations register, and who maintains it?

interviewGuides.question: What are the key compliance breaches, incidents or audit findings of the last two years, and their root causes?
interviewGuides.probe: Are there recurring themes?

interviewGuides.question: How well do the three lines of accountability work in practice?
interviewGuides.probe: Where do roles overlap or leave gaps?

interviewGuides.question: How resilient are critical operations, and when were BCP and DR arrangements last tested?
interviewGuides.probe: Results and actions from the last test.

interviewGuides.question: How are third-party and supplier risks managed?
interviewGuides.probe: Are material service providers identified?

interviewGuides.question: What regulatory changes on the horizon will affect the operating model?
interviewGuides.probe: How is regulatory change tracked?

interviewGuides.question: What is the sourcing strategy, and how are make, buy and partner decisions made?
interviewGuides.probe: Who has the final say?

interviewGuides.question: Who are the critical and strategic suppliers, and where is concentration risk?
interviewGuides.probe: Are there single-source dependencies?

interviewGuides.question: How are contracts and supplier performance managed?
interviewGuides.probe: Are scorecards and regular reviews in place?

interviewGuides.question: How efficient and compliant is the procurement process?
interviewGuides.probe: Typical cycle times and bottlenecks.

interviewGuides.question: Which major contracts are due for renewal in the next 24 months, and are they aligned to the future operating model?
interviewGuides.probe: Opportunities to consolidate or renegotiate.

interviewGuides.question: How are supplier security and privacy risks assessed?
interviewGuides.probe: Before engagement and during the contract term.

interviewGuides.question: What do you value most about the organisation's services?
interviewGuides.probe: What would you miss if it stopped?

interviewGuides.question: What are your biggest frustrations when dealing with the organisation?
interviewGuides.probe: A recent example.

interviewGuides.question: How easy is it to get things done across channels (online, phone, in person)?
interviewGuides.probe: Do you have to repeat information?

interviewGuides.question: How well does the organisation communicate and follow through on its commitments?
interviewGuides.probe: Examples of commitments kept or missed.

interviewGuides.question: How does the organisation compare with others you deal with?
interviewGuides.probe: Who does this well?

interviewGuides.question: What should the organisation start, stop or continue doing?

interviewNote: Opening and closing (use in every interview): explain the purpose and confidentiality of the interview; ask the interviewee to describe their role; close by asking 'What have I not asked that I should have?' and 'Who else should we speak to?'.

finding.finding: Investment decisions below $250k are escalated to the Executive Committee, adding four to six weeks to minor change.
finding.rootCause: Delegations not updated since the 2019 restructure
finding.impact: Slower delivery of minor change; executive time spent on low-value decisions

recommendation.recommendation: Refresh delegations of authority to align with the current structure and risk appetite, devolving investment decisions below $250k to business unit heads.
recommendation.benefits: Faster delivery of minor change; executive time refocused on strategic decisions
recommendation.risks: Weaker control if delegations are not system-enforced
